title: Rethinking Geometric Depth in Monocular 3D Object Detection: A Projection-Consistent Reformulation
claim: A standard geometric depth formula is systematically biased because projection makes it recover front-surface depth, and the error grows with object size.
layout: 2 panels, left bar chart then right geometry diagram, labeled math symbols
description: The figure has two panels. Panel (a) is a grouped bar chart of depth MAE in metres for four categories: Pedestrian, Cyclist, Car and Truck. Blue bars show GeoDepth and orange bars show PCDepth (Ours). The blue bars grow with object size, from 0.48 for Pedestrian to 4.82 for Truck. The orange bars stay low, from 0.26 to 1.03. Panel (b) is a side-view perspective-projection sketch. A line-drawn car sits on a ground line, and a camera at the right sends dashed rays to coloured points: red for the 3D bottom center, green for the occluding point, and yellow for the visible bottom. Blue arrows mark z, f, H and h. Two small image-plane insets on the far right show the car's front view with h'_2D and h_2D. The eye goes first to the tall blue Truck bar.
caption: (a) Depth error under ideal inputs. We evaluate the GeoDepth formulation [71] using ground-truth f, H, and h2D. Even with these oracle inputs, GeoDepth incurs a non-trivial error that grows with object scale, revealing a structural rather than statistical bias. Our PCDepth substantially mitigates this bias across all categories. (b) Geometric origin of the bias. Under perspective projection, the 3D bottom center (red) is self-occluded by a nearer surface point (green) that projects higher on the image plane, while the visible bottom in the image corresponds to a still-closer surface point (yellow). The commonly adopted formulation z = f · H/h2D therefore recovers the depth of the visible front surface rather than that of the object center, systematically underestimating depth.
abstract: Monocular 3D detection (Mono3D) hinges on recovering depth from a single image, for which the geometric formulation $z \approx f \cdot H / h_{2D}$ is widely adopted due to its simplicity and direct grounding in projective geometry. We show that this formulation harbors a systematic, projection-induced bias: substituting the 2D bounding-box height $h_{2D}$ recovers the depth of an object's visible front surface rather than its center, causing size-dependent underestimation that persists even under ground-truth inputs. We address this front-surface bias with MonoPCA, a unified framework built on a projection-consistent reformulation. At its core, PCDepth retains the measurable $h_{2D}$ and closes the gap to center depth through an orientation- and size-aware correction derived from perspective geometry, eliminating the bias without introducing ill-posed regression targets. Because PCDepth couples depth to predicted object size and orientation, attribute perception becomes essential. We therefore introduce GeoAlign, a teacher-student framework that transfers geometric representations from Vision Foundation Models into a lightweight student, strengthening attribute perception at no inference cost. Across four challenging benchmarks, MonoPCA achieves SoTA performance, including a +1.44% AP$_{3D}$ gain on the KITTI leaderboard and +2.80% on Omni3D$_{OUT}$. Code is available at https://github.com/alanzhangcs/MonoPCA.
